input.name: bipartiteTimeline
input.task: Events change an undirected graph on the nodes 1..n. An "add" event adds an edge and gives it the next number: 1 for the first add event, 2 for the second, and so on. An edge between u and u (a loop) is allowed, and two edges between the same pair of nodes are two different edges (parallel edges). A "del" event removes the edge with that number if it is in the graph now; nothing happens when it was removed before or when no edge has that number yet. A removed edge is never added again. A "query" event records two facts about the graph as it is at that moment: components, the number of connected components, counting every node (an isolated node is a component); and flag, which is 1 when the graph is bipartite and 0 when it is not. A graph is bipartite when its nodes can be coloured with two colours so that every edge joins two different colours, so a loop makes it not bipartite, and so does any cycle of odd length. Return the sum over the queries of q * (2 * components + flag), where q is 1 for the first query, 2 for the second, and so on. When there is no query, return 0. events is either an array of explicit events, each of them ["add", u, v], ["del", k] or ["query"] (then seed is ignored), or an integer m, and then m events are generated from seed. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). For each event it draws three consecutive terms a, b, c, in this order, and kind = a mod 8. For kind 0, 1 or 2 it is an add event with u = (b mod n) + 1 and v = (c mod n) + 1, except that when floor(a / 8) mod 1500 is not 0 and u and v are both odd or both even, v is replaced by (v mod n) + 1 (n is even in this form, so the edge then joins an odd and an even node). For kind 3 it is a del event with k = (b mod A) + 1, where A is the number of add events so far; when A is 0 the event is skipped. For kinds 4 to 7 it is a query event. Limits: explicit form 1 <= n <= 1000 and at most 1000 events; generated form n even with 2 <= n <= 40000, 1 <= m <= 60000 and 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. The inputs are too large for any method that rebuilds the graph for every query.

edges.isolated: an isolated node is a component

input.name: resolveDeps
input.task: Write a dependency resolver. resolveDeps(registry, root) returns the versions to install, or null. registry maps a package name to an object that maps each version of the package to the dependencies of that version, for example { "a": { "1.0.0": { "b": "^1.2.0" }, "1.1.0": {} } }. A dependency is a package name with a range string. root is an object of the same kind: the ranges that the user asks for. The keys of every dependency object are in the order in which the dependencies are listed. Versions. A version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, three integers of 0 or more, with an optional prerelease: a hyphen and dot-separated identifiers of letters and digits, as in "1.2.3-beta.2". Versions are ordered by MAJOR, then MINOR, then PATCH. With equal numbers, a version with a prerelease is lower than the same version without one. Two prereleases are compared identifier by identifier from the left: two numeric identifiers (digits only) by their number; a numeric identifier is lower than an identifier with a letter; two identifiers with letters in plain character order; when all shared identifiers are equal, the one with fewer identifiers is lower. Ranges. A range is one or more alternatives separated by "||"; a version satisfies the range when it satisfies at least one alternative. An alternative is comparators separated by spaces (all must hold), or two versions with " - " between them (a hyphen range). A blank alternative holds for any version (but see the prerelease rule). Spaces around an alternative are ignored. A comparator is an optional operator followed by a version, with no space between them. A partial version has 1 or 2 numbers ("1", "1.2"), or has an x, X or * in place of the minor or patch number ("1.x", "1.2.*"); the parts that are not given are wild. "*", "x" and "X" alone match any version. The comparators: (1) No operator, or "=": a full version matches itself (its prerelease must be equal); a partial version matches every version from its lowest (the missing parts are 0) up to, but not including, the next one: "1.2" means >=1.2.0 and <1.3.0, and "1" means >=1.0.0 and <2.0.0. (2) ">=" and "<" compare with the version, a partial version being filled with 0. (3) ">": for a full version, higher than it; for a partial version, the next version or higher: ">1.2" is >=1.3.0 and ">1" is >=2.0.0. (4) "<=": for a full version, at most it; for a partial version, lower than the next version: "<=1.2" is <1.3.0. (5) "!=": different from a full version; for a partial version, outside the range that it means without an operator, so "!=1.2" excludes every 1.2.x. (6) "~": at least the version (filled with 0) and below the next minor version ("~1.2.3" and "~1.2" mean <1.3.0), or below the next major version when only the major number is given ("~1" means <2.0.0). (7) "^": at least the version (filled with 0) and below the next version that changes the left-most non-zero number among the numbers given: ^1.2.3 is <2.0.0, ^0.2.3 is <0.3.0, ^0.0.3 is <0.0.4, ^1.2 is <2.0.0, ^0.0 is <0.1.0 and ^0 is <1.0.0. A hyphen range "A - B" means at least A (filled with 0), and at most B for a full B, or below the next version of B for a partial B: "1.2.3 - 2.3" means >=1.2.3 and <2.4.0. Prerelease rule. A version with a prerelease satisfies an alternative only if all its comparators hold and at least one comparator of that alternative has a prerelease on a full version with the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbers. A "!=" comparator never counts for this, and in a hyphen range both of its versions count. A version without a prerelease needs only the comparators. Resolution. Pick one version for each package that is needed, so that every range required for a package holds for the picked version, by this exact search. Keep a list of package names in the order in which they are first required: first the keys of root, in their order. Whenever a package gets a version, the dependencies of that version are required, and a dependency that is not in the list yet is added to the end of the list. The search goes through the list in order, one package per step. At the step of a package, the candidates are the versions in registry that satisfy all ranges required for the package so far (by root and by the packages that were picked before), highest version first. Try each candidate in turn: pick it and require its dependencies; if one of its dependencies is a package that is already picked and the picked version does not satisfy the new range, or if the later steps fail, undo this pick (and the ranges and list entries it added) and go on with the next candidate. If no candidate works, the step fails, and the step before it goes on with its next candidate. A package that is not in registry has no candidates. The search ends when every package in the list has a version. The result is null when the first step fails. Otherwise it is an array of [name, version] pairs, sorted by name in plain character order, one for each picked package.

edges.blank: A blank alternative holds for any version
edges.prerelease-order: a numeric identifier is lower than an identifier with a letter
edges.prerelease-rule: at least one comparator of that alternative has a prerelease
edges.order: in the order in which they are first required
edges.missing: A package that is not in registry has no candidates
edges.null: The result is null when the first step fails

input.name: distinctSquareSum
input.task: A sequence a_1, ..., a_n is built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). The value a_i (i = 1..n) is x_i mod v, so every value is an integer from 0 to v - 1. Every value x has a weight w(x) = (x mod 7) + 1. For a subarray a_l, ..., a_r (1 <= l <= r <= n), let D(l, r) be the sum of w(x) over the distinct values x that occur in the subarray. A value that occurs several times in the subarray counts once. Return the sum of D(l, r) * D(l, r) over all pairs 1 <= l <= r <= n, modulo 1000000007, as a number. Limits: 1 <= n <= 200000; 1 <= v <= 200000; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. The inputs are too large for any method that visits every pair of start and end positions.

tier.basis: The reference is about 55 lines: a closed form for the sum of squares over all subarrays (a diagonal term and a pair term whose left bound is max(p_i, p_j)), prefix sums for one part of the pair term and a Fenwick tree for the other; the derivation is where an expert spends an hour, the code is short.

input.name: standings
input.task: Build the table of a football league. standings(rules, teams, events) returns the teams in table order. rules is { win, draw, goals, bonus }: win and draw are the points for a win and a draw, goals is the number of goals that earns a bonus, and bonus is the number of points for each bonus (all are integers of 0 or more). teams is an array of unique team names. events is an array that is read in order; the table is built from the matches that are stored at the end. Events: ["match", id, home, away, homeGoals, awayGoals]; ["award", id, home, away, side], where side is "H" or "A" and the match counts as a 3-0 win for that side; ["void", id]; ["deduct", team, points]; ["card", team, points]. Matches. A match or award event stores the match under its id; a later match or award event with the same id replaces the stored one, and a void event removes it (a void for an id that is not stored does nothing). A stored match that names a team that is not in teams is ignored. A deduct or card event for a team that is not in teams is ignored. A team has played one game for each stored match it takes part in. Points of a match. A team gets win points for a win, draw points for a draw and 0 for a loss. For a match event (not for an award) it also gets bonus points when it scored goals goals or more, and bonus points again when it lost by exactly one goal; both can apply to the same team in one match. An award counts as 3 goals for and 0 goals against for the winner, 0 for and 3 against for the other team, and gives no bonus points. Totals. The total of a team is the sum of its points from all its matches minus the sum of the points of all its deduct events (it can be below 0). The card points of a team are the sum of its card events. GD is goals for minus goals against over all its matches, and GF is its goals for. Order. Teams are ordered by total, the most first. Teams with equal totals form a group, and each group is ordered like this. Take only the matches between two teams of the group (a mini-league; deductions do not count there) and, for each team, the points of those matches, the GD of those matches and the GF of those matches. Order the group by mini-league points, then mini-league GD, then mini-league GF, the most first. Teams that are equal on all three stay together as a subgroup. If the mini-league splits the group into more than one subgroup, every subgroup of two or more teams is ordered again in the same way, with the mini-league of that subgroup only (its own matches). If it does not split the group (all teams are equal on all three), the group is ordered by overall GD, then overall GF, the most first, then by fewer card points, then by team name in plain character order (a < b), the first first. The result is an array with one row [team, played, total, GD, GF] per team, in table order. A team with no matches has the row [team, 0, its total, 0, 0].

edges.bonus: both can apply to the same team in one match
edges.void: a void for an id that is not stored does nothing
edges.unknown-team: names a team that is not in teams is ignored
edges.deduct: minus the sum of the points of all its deduct events
edges.recursion: ordered again in the same way
edges.no-split: If it does not split the group
edges.name: in plain character order

input.name: runOrderBook
input.task: Write a matching engine for one instrument. runOrderBook(config, events) processes the events in order and returns { results, trades, book }. config is { tick, lot, band }: tick and lot are positive integers and band is an integer of 0 or more (a percentage). All prices and quantities are integers. Events are arrays: ["limit", id, account, side, price, qty, tif, display], ["market", id, account, side, qty], ["cancel", id] and ["replace", id, price, qty]. id and account are strings. side is "B" (buy) or "S" (sell). tif is "GTC", "IOC", "FOK" or "POST". display is a positive integer or null; a limit event may leave display out, which means null. Resting orders. An order that rests in the book has a price, a visible size and a hidden size. The orders at one price form a queue; a new resting order joins the end of the queue of its price. A resting order from a limit event whose display is smaller than its remaining quantity is an iceberg: its visible size is display and its hidden size is remaining minus display. Any other resting order has visible size = remaining quantity and hidden size 0. An order keeps its display value for as long as it is in the book. Matching. An incoming buy order trades with resting sell orders whose price is at most its limit price, lowest price first. An incoming sell order trades with resting buy orders whose price is at least its limit price, highest price first. A market order has no limit price and can trade at any price. Within one price, the order at the front of the queue goes first. Take the resting order r at the front of the best acceptable price. If r has the same account as the incoming order, r is removed from the book without a trade and matching goes on. Otherwise they trade q = the smaller of the incoming remaining quantity and the visible size of r, at the price of r. The trade is recorded as [buyId, sellId, price, q], and its price becomes the last trade price. When the visible size of r reaches 0 and r has a hidden size, r shows min(display, hidden size) from its hidden part and moves to the end of the queue of its price; without a hidden size, r is removed. Matching stops when the incoming remaining quantity is 0 or no acceptable resting order is left. Checks. A limit or market event is checked before it matches, in this order, and the first failure rejects it with the result "reject:<reason>" and no change to the book. "dup": id is the id of an order that rests in the book now (an id may be used again after its order has left the book). "lot": qty, or a display that is not null, is not a positive multiple of lot. "tick" (limit events only): price is not a positive multiple of tick. "band" (limit events only): a trade has happened and |price - last| * 100 > last * band, where last is the last trade price. Time in force of a limit event. "GTC": what is left after matching rests in the book. "IOC": what is left is dropped. "FOK": before matching, add the total size (visible plus hidden) of the resting orders on the other side that are acceptable for it and have a different account; if that sum is less than qty, the event is rejected with "reject:fok" and the book does not change; otherwise it matches as usual. "POST": if a resting order on the other side has a price that the incoming order could trade with, whatever its account, the event is rejected with "reject:post"; otherwise it rests without matching. A market event is dropped like IOC for what is left. A display on an IOC or FOK event is ignored after the check. Results. For a limit or market event that is not rejected, the result is "filled:N" when all of qty traded; otherwise "rested:N" when what is left was put in the book; otherwise "expired:N". N is the quantity that traded. "cancel" removes the resting order with that id and gives "cancelled:N", where N is its visible size plus its hidden size. An id that is not in the book gives "reject:unknown". "replace" gives the resting order id a new price and a new total quantity qty. Checks, in this order: "unknown" (the id is not in the book), "lot" (qty is not a positive multiple of lot), "tick" (price is not a positive multiple of tick) and "band" (as above, with the new price). A failed check changes nothing. If the new price equals the current price and qty is not more than the current total (visible plus hidden), the order keeps its place in the queue and loses the difference from its hidden size first, then from its visible size; the result is "replaced:0". Otherwise the order is removed and enters again as a GTC order with the same id, account, side and display, and the new price and quantity: it matches like an incoming limit order and what is left joins the end of the queue (there is no "dup" check). The result is "replaced:N", where N is the quantity that traded. Output. results holds one string per event. trades lists the trades in order. book is [bids, asks]; each list holds [id, price, visible plus hidden size] for every resting order, bids from the highest price and asks from the lowest price, and within one price in queue order.

edges.price-time: Within one price, the order at the front of the queue goes first
edges.self-trade: removed from the book without a trade
edges.iceberg: moves to the end of the queue of its price
edges.lot-display: a display that is not null
edges.cancel: visible size plus its hidden size
edges.replace-keep: loses the difference from its hidden size first
edges.replace-requeue: enters again as a GTC order

input.name: repeatedPalindromes
input.task: Count the palindromic substrings of a string S that are long enough and occur at least twice. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. Count each distinct palindromic substring P once, when its length is at least minLen and it occurs in S at least twice. Occurrences are counted by their start position and may overlap: the string "aa" occurs twice in "aaa". A single letter is a palindrome. source is either the string S itself (lower-case letters), or an object { n, alphabet, runMax, seed } that describes S, so that the input stays small. For the object form, S is built from runs of one letter. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Repeat until S has n characters: draw the next term x and take the letter with index (x mod alphabet) (the letters are "a", "b", "c", ... in order); draw the next term y and take the run length (y mod runMax) + 1; append that many copies of the letter, but only as many as are needed to make S exactly n characters long. Two neighbouring runs may have the same letter. Return the count as a number. Limits: for the string form, 1 <= length of S <= 1000. For the object form, 1 <= n <= 200000, 1 <= alphabet <= 26, 1 <= runMax <= 200000 and 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. 1 <= minLen <= 200000. The inputs are too large for any method that visits every palindrome occurrence one by one.

edges.distinct: Count each distinct palindromic substring P once
edges.min-length: its length is at least minLen
edges.letter: A single letter is a palindrome

tier.name: extra-hard
tier.basis: The reference is about 65 lines: a palindromic tree (suffix links by a second walk, one node per distinct palindrome) with the occurrence counts pushed along the suffix links in reverse order of creation; the structure is known, but the link walk and the count propagation take an expert more than an hour to write and check.

input.name: reassemble
input.task: Write the receiver of a small packet protocol, "slip". reassemble(config, packets) returns { streams, drops }. config is { window, timeout }: both are integers of 1 or more. packets is an array of packets, processed in the given order; the times in it never decrease. A packet is [time, stream, seq, flags, payload, check]: time and seq are integers, stream is a string, flags is a string, payload is a string of printable ASCII characters (it may be empty), and check is an integer. The flags are letters: "S" (start), "F" (final) and "R" (reset). flags may be empty, and a letter may repeat. Every packet carries bytes: payload byte i has the position pos + i, where pos = seq - base, and base is the seq of the packet that started the stream. Step 1, expiry. Before a packet is looked at, every open stream that has had no accepted packet for timeout time units or more (packet time - last accepted time >= timeout) times out: its status becomes "timeout", it is closed, and its bytes that are not delivered yet are discarded. This happens for every packet, also for one that is dropped later. Step 2, check. The sum of the character codes of payload, plus the character codes of flags, plus 31 * seq, modulo 251, must equal check. A packet that fails is dropped, counted under "check", and has no other effect. Step 3, flags. A packet is dropped, counted under "flags", when flags has a letter other than S, F and R, or when it has R together with any other letter. Step 4, stream. Streams are found by their id, among the open ones. A packet with S for a stream that is open is dropped and counted under "restart". A packet with S for a stream that is not open opens a new stream with base = seq, delivered text "", status "open", 0 conflicts, and its last accepted time is time. Every stream that is opened is listed in streams, in the order it was opened, so one id can appear several times. A packet without S for a stream that is not open (never opened, done, reset or timed out) is dropped and counted under "orphan". A packet with R resets the open stream: its status becomes "reset", it is closed, the payload is ignored, and what was delivered so far stays as its text. Step 5, position. A packet with pos below 0 is dropped and counted under "old". A packet with F whose end position pos + payload length is smaller than the number of bytes already delivered is dropped and counted under "badend". Every other packet is accepted: the stream's last accepted time becomes time, also when the packet adds nothing new. Step 6, bytes. The end of the stream is unknown until a packet with F is accepted; then the end is pos + payload length of that packet. If the end is already known, the F flag of a later packet is ignored. A byte at a position that is the end or more is ignored. Let next be the number of bytes delivered so far; a byte at a position of next + window or more is also ignored (next is taken before this packet delivers anything). A byte that is not ignored is stored. If a byte for that position was already received (delivered or stored), the first one stays; if the new byte differs from it, the conflicts of the stream grow by 1. Step 7, delivery. After the bytes of a packet are handled, stored bytes are delivered while the byte at position next exists and next is below the end (if the end is known): each one is appended to the text of the stream, and next grows by 1. When the end is known and next equals the end, the status becomes "done" and the stream is closed. A packet with S and F and an empty payload therefore gives a done stream with an empty text at once. The result: streams is an array of [id, text, status, conflicts] for every stream that was opened; a stream that is still open at the end of packets has status "open" (no expiry is run at the end). drops is { check, orphan, restart, flags, old, badend } with the number of packets dropped for each reason, in this key order.

edges.expiry: packet time - last accepted time >= timeout
edges.expiry-on-drop: also for one that is dropped later
edges.reset: what was delivered so far stays as its text
edges.generation: so one id can appear several times
edges.badend: smaller than the number of bytes already delivered
edges.refresh: also when the packet adds nothing new
edges.end-once: the F flag of a later packet is ignored
edges.beyond-end: the end or more is ignored
edges.window: next is taken before this packet delivers anything
edges.delivery: while the byte at position next exists
edges.open-at-end: no expiry is run at the end

tier.name: extra-hard
tier.basis: estimated from the reference (about 80 lines): a receiver with seven fixed steps, a window measured before delivery, first-byte-wins conflicts, an end that is set once, expiry that runs on dropped packets and a new stream for a reused id; the time is the careful reading of about 25 rules and the checks of the order in which they apply

input.name: playCairn
input.task:
Implement playCairn(setup, actions), the referee of a two-player stacking game called Cairn. It plays a list of attempted actions and returns the final report. Players are "A" and "B". setup is an object { rows, reserve, first, relics, zones }. rows is an array of 1 to 8 strings of the same length (1 to 8 characters): the board. reserve is a whole number from 0 to 12: the number of discs each player holds in reserve at the start. first is "A" or "B": the player who acts first. relics is an optional array of cell names (see BOARD); when it is missing there are no relics. zones is an optional array of objects { cells, bonus }: cells is an array of 1 or more cell names (none of them a wall, all on the board) and bonus is a whole number from 1 to 9; when it is missing there are no zones. actions is an array of strings, one attempted action each.

BOARD. A cell is named by one lowercase column letter followed by a row number without leading zeros. Column "a" is the first character of each string of rows and row 1 is the first string of rows, so "c2" is the character with index 2 of rows[1]. A cell name that is well formed but lies outside the board is off-board. The character of a cell gives its terrain and its capacity (the largest height a tower may have there): "." plain, capacity 4; "~" marsh, capacity 4; "*" shrine, capacity 4; "^" ridge, capacity 2; "=" bridge, capacity 3; "#" wall, capacity 0 (a wall never holds a disc). All cells start empty. Every relic named in setup.relics is a cell that is not a wall.

TOWERS. A cell holds a tower: a list of discs from bottom to top, each owned by A or B. The height is the number of discs. The controller of a tower is the owner of its top disc (an empty cell has no controller). The top run of a tower is the number of discs, counted from the top down, that have the same owner as the top disc. A tower is sealed when its height equals the capacity of its cell and all its discs have the same owner (so two discs of one owner on a ridge are sealed; an empty cell is never sealed). A disc that is "removed from the game" is gone for good and is not returned to a reserve.

ACTION TEXT. An action string consists of tokens separated by exactly one space, with no space at the start or the end. A cell token is one lowercase letter a-z followed by a number without leading zeros and at least 1 (so "a0", "a01", "A1", "aa1" and "a1x" are not cell tokens). A count token is a whole number from 1 to 999999 without leading zeros. The forms are: "put CELL", "go CELL CELL COUNT", "swap CELL CELL", "run CELL CELL CELL" with 3, 4 or 5 cell tokens in all, "lift CELL", "fort CELL" and "pass". Any other string is bad-format: an unknown verb, a wrong number of tokens, a token that is not well formed, an extra or a missing space, a letter in the wrong case. A string with the right form whose cell is outside the board is not bad-format; it fails the off-board check below.

TURNS. Actions are played in the order of the array. The player named by first acts first. After every action that is played, whether it was legal or not, the turn passes to the other player. The player whose turn it is is the actor of the action.

LEGAL ACTIONS. An action that is not bad-format is legal when it passes every check listed for its verb. The checks are made in the order given, and the first check that fails is the reason of the fault. A legal action then has its effect.
- put CELL (the actor places one disc from the actor's reserve). Checks: (1) off-board; (2) wall: the cell is a wall; (3) no-build: the cell is a bridge; (4) no-reserve: the actor's reserve is 0; (5) enemy-held: the controller of the cell is the opponent; (6) full: the height equals the capacity; (7) guarded: the cell is empty and at least one of its orthogonal neighbours (up, down, left, right; those that exist) has the opponent as controller and a height of at least 3. Effect: the reserve of the actor falls by 1 and a disc of the actor is placed on top of the tower.
- go FROM TO COUNT (the actor moves the top COUNT discs of one tower onto the tower of a neighbouring cell). Checks: (1) off-board: either cell is outside the board; (2) not-adjacent: FROM and TO are not orthogonal neighbours (the same cell twice is not adjacent); (3) wall: either cell is a wall; (4) empty: FROM holds no disc; (5) not-yours: the controller of FROM is the opponent; (6) sealed: FROM is sealed; (7) too-many: COUNT is more than the height of FROM; (8) full: height(TO) + COUNT is more than the capacity of TO; (9) if the controller of TO is the opponent: (9a) sealed: TO is sealed; (9b) too-weak: COUNT is less than the top run of TO, plus 1 more when TO is a shrine, plus 1 more when TO has a fort that belongs to the opponent (see fort). Effect: the top COUNT discs leave FROM as one block. If the controller of TO is the opponent, this is an assault and the top disc of TO (the one under the landing block, taken before the block lands) is converted: it now belongs to the actor. Then the block is put on top of TO in the same order (the disc that was on top of FROM is on top of TO).
- swap FIRST SECOND (the actor exchanges two whole towers). Checks: (1) off-board; (2) not-adjacent; (3) wall; (4) empty: either cell holds no disc; (5) not-yours: either tower has the opponent as controller; (6) sealed: either tower is sealed; (7) full: the height of one tower is more than the capacity of the other cell. Effect: the two lists of discs change places.
- run C1 C2 ... Ck (the actor sends the top disc of the first tower along a path of k cells, 3 <= k <= 5). Checks: (1) off-board: any cell; (2) not-adjacent: two cells that follow each other in the path are not orthogonal neighbours; (3) wall: any cell; (4) empty: C1 holds no disc; (5) not-yours: the controller of C1 is the opponent; (6) sealed: C1 is sealed; (7) repeat: a cell occurs twice in the path; (8) blocked: some cell strictly between C1 and Ck has the opponent as controller or has a height equal to its capacity; (9) full: Ck has a height equal to its capacity; (10) if the controller of Ck is the opponent: (10a) sealed: Ck is sealed; (10b) too-weak: the top run of Ck, plus 1 more when Ck is a shrine, plus 1 more when Ck has a fort that belongs to the opponent, is more than 1. Effect: the top disc of C1 is taken off. Let w be the number of marsh cells among C2 ... Ck. If w is 2 or more the disc drowns: it is removed from the game and nothing else changes. Otherwise, if the controller of Ck is the opponent, the top disc of Ck is converted (it now belongs to the actor) as in an assault by go; then the disc is put on top of Ck. The cells between are not changed.
- lift CELL (the actor takes the top disc back). Checks: (1) off-board; (2) wall; (3) empty; (4) not-yours; (5) sealed; (6) too-low: the height is less than 2. Effect: the top disc is removed from the tower and the reserve of the actor rises by 1.
- fort CELL (the actor builds a fort on a tower). Checks: (1) off-board; (2) wall; (3) no-build: the cell is a bridge; (4) no-reserve: the reserve of the actor is less than 2; (5) empty; (6) not-yours; (7) fortified: the cell already has a fort (of either player); (8) too-many-forts: the actor already owns 2 forts. Effect: the reserve of the actor falls by 2 (those discs are removed from the game) and the cell gets a fort that belongs to the actor for the rest of the game, whoever controls the tower later. A fort changes no tower, so no sinking, collapse or monument step follows it, but it is a legal action that counts for the EVENTS below. A tide or a storm does nothing to a cell that has a fort.
- pass is always legal and has no effect.

FAULTS. An action that is bad-format or has a failed check is a fault of its actor. It changes nothing on the board. The fault is logged as the text "N:reason", where N is the 1-based position of the action in the array and reason is the name used above (for example "7:wall"; "bad-format" for the case of the ACTION TEXT section). The faults of a player are counted.

AFTER A LEGAL PUT, GO, SWAP OR RUN. Let the changed cells be: for put, the cell; for go, TO; for swap, FIRST and then SECOND; for run, Ck when the disc was put there (none when it drowned). Step 1, sinking: for every changed cell that is a marsh, while the height is more than 2 the bottom disc is removed from the game. Step 2, collapse: for every changed cell that is a bridge, if the height is 3 and the three discs do not all have the same owner, all three discs are removed from the game (a bridge with three discs of one owner stays; it is sealed). Step 3, monuments: for every changed cell in the order above, if the tower is sealed and that cell has not been a monument before, the cell becomes a monument and the reserve of the controller rises by 1 (a cell can be a monument once in the whole game, even if it is sealed again later). Steps 1 and 2 are done for all changed cells (in the order above) before step 3 starts, and step 3 uses the towers as they are after steps 1 and 2.
A lift and a fort change no cell for these steps: neither sinking nor collapse nor monuments happen after them.

EVENTS. Count the legal actions that are not a pass, over both players, starting with 1 (a fault and a pass are not counted). After the steps above, for the legal action with count c: if c is a multiple of 4, the tide happens: every marsh tower of height 2 or more loses its bottom disc (removed from the game). Then, if c is a multiple of 6, the harvest happens: for every cell that is a shrine or a relic (a cell that is both counts once) whose tower has a controller, the harvest score of that controller rises by 1. Then, if c is a multiple of 8, the supply happens: each player who controls 3 or more towers gets 1 more disc in the reserve. Then, if c is a multiple of 10, the storm happens: on every ridge whose tower is not empty and not sealed, the top disc is removed from the game. Several events at one count happen in this order: tide, harvest, supply, storm. (The tide and the storm skip a cell that has a fort.)

END OF THE GAME. A legal pass makes the pass streak one higher, and any other legal action sets the streak to 0; faults do not change the streak. The game ends at once, with the action just played as the last one, in these cases: when the streak is 2 (ended "passes"); when the fault just logged is the third fault of its actor (ended "forfeit", and that actor is the forfeiter). When the actions are used up, the game ends with ended "actions". Actions after the end are not played and not counted.

SCORING. The score of a player is the sum of: (a) tower points for every tower that the player controls: let h be the height; the base is h; on a shrine it is 2h; on a marsh it is floor(h / 2); on a ridge it is h + 1; on a bridge it is max(0, h - 1); on plain it is h. Then add 3 if the tower is sealed, then add 2 if the cell is a relic, then add 2 if the cell has a fort that belongs to the controller of the tower. (b) The chain bonus: consider the cells whose tower the player controls; two such cells are connected when they are orthogonal neighbours; let s be the size of the largest connected group of such cells; the bonus is 2 * (s - 1) when s >= 2, else 0. (c) floor(reserve / 2) for the reserve the player has at the end. (d) the harvest score of the player. (e) minus 2 for every fault of the player. (f) the zone bonuses: for each zone, count for each player how many cells of the zone hold a tower that the player controls; if the counts are equal, nobody gets the bonus; otherwise the player with the larger count gets the bonus of the zone, doubled when that count is equal to the number of cells of the zone and the zone has at least 2 cells. The score can be negative. The winner is: when the game ended by forfeit, the player who is not the forfeiter, whatever the scores are; otherwise the player with the higher score; with equal scores the player who controls more towers; if that is equal too, "draw".

RESULT. Return an object with these keys: rows: an array of strings, one per row of the board; in a row the cells are written from the first column to the last and joined by "|"; a wall is "#", an empty cell that is not a wall is "-", any other cell is its discs from bottom to top as letters (for example "ABB"). reserve: { A, B } the reserves at the end. score: { A, B } the final scores. faults: the array of fault texts in order. played: the number of actions played. ended: "passes", "forfeit" or "actions". winner: "A", "B" or "draw".

edges.sinking: while the height is more than 2 the bottom disc is removed from the game

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A referee for an invented stacking game: an action parser, five verbs with ordered legality checks (about 40 reasons), sinking, monuments, tide, harvest and storm events counted over legal actions, a scoring rule with four terrain formulas, a connected-group bonus and a forfeit rule. The reference is about 450 lines. An expert needs a full working day to read about 60 stated rules closely, write the referee and check it against worked examples.

input.name: maxCappedProfit
input.signature: maxCappedProfit(m, n, blocks, maxCap, maxLen, maxProfit, seed) -> number
input.task: A road has m positions numbered 0..m-1. n offers each want a stretch of it, and the road has a capacity at every position. The capacities and the offers are built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. Step 1: for b = 0..blocks-1, draw r and set capacity(b) = r mod (maxCap + 1). Block b holds the positions from floor(b * m / blocks) to floor((b + 1) * m / blocks) - 1, and every position of block b has the capacity capacity(b). The capacity can differ from block to block, and a capacity of 0 is allowed. Step 2: for i = 0..n-1, draw r1, r2, r3 in this order and set l = r1 mod m, r = min(m, l + 1 + (r2 mod maxLen)) and profit = 1 + (r3 mod maxProfit). Offer i covers the positions l, l+1, ..., r-1; the end r itself is not covered, so two offers that only touch at an end do not overlap. Several offers can be identical. Choose a set of offers (the empty set is allowed). At every position x, the number of chosen offers that cover x must be at most the capacity of x. A position with capacity 0 may not be covered by any chosen offer. The score of a choice is the sum of the profits of the chosen offers. Return the largest possible score. Because offers compete for capacity, it can be better to skip the most profitable offer, and an offer that covers a position with capacity 0 can never be chosen. Limits: 1 <= m <= 200000; 1 <= n <= 20000; 1 <= blocks <= min(m, 12); 0 <= maxCap <= 6; 1 <= maxLen <= m; 1 <= maxProfit <= 1000000; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. The score is an exact integer below 2^53. The number of subsets of offers is far too large to try, and choosing the most profitable offers first is not always right.

edges.half-open: the end r itself is not covered
edges.trade-off: it can be better to skip the most profitable offer
edges.varying: the capacity can differ from block to block

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Interval selection with a capacity that changes along the road is a min-cost flow, but not the textbook one: the capacity differs from block to block, so the reduction needs a supply or demand at every point where the capacity changes (a lower bound on the idle edge), negative costs for the offers, and shortest paths with potentials. Greedy by profit is wrong, and the exact search over subsets is exponential (30 offers already take several seconds, 60 take minutes). About 5 h for an expert who has seen the reduction before.

input.name: conflictLedger
input.signature: conflictLedger(n, q, reach, removeTenths, seed) -> number
input.task: A network of n stations numbered 0..n-1 starts with no links. A list of q operations adds links, removes links and asks questions. The operations are built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. For each operation, in order, draw three numbers r1, r2, r3 (always all three, whatever the operation does) and set kind = r1 mod 10. If kind >= 7, the operation is a question (kinds 7, 8 and 9). Let w = r2 mod n. If kind is from 7 - removeTenths to 6, the operation is a removal. Keep a list of the links that exist, in the order in which they were added. If the list is empty, nothing happens. Otherwise let i = r2 mod (the length of the list), delete the link at position i, and let the removal move the last link of the list into its place (when i is the last position, the list just gets shorter). The order of the list is therefore not the order of adding once a link has been removed. Otherwise (kind <= 6 - removeTenths) the operation adds a link: u = r2 mod n, v = (u + (r3 mod reach)) mod n, and the link joins u and v. u may equal v (a self-loop). A link is an unordered pair of stations, and at most one link per pair exists: a link that already exists is not added again, and then the list stays as it is. A link that was removed can be added again later, and goes to the end of the list. A component is a maximal set of stations that are joined by links; a station with no link is a component of its own. A component is odd when it contains a cycle of odd length. A self-loop is an odd cycle (of length 1), a triangle is an odd cycle, and a cycle of even length is not an odd cycle. For a question, look at the links that exist at that moment and compute four numbers: a1 = the number of components, a2 = the number of stations that belong to odd components, a3 = the number of stations in the component of station w, a4 = 1 if the component of w is odd and 0 if not. Fold the answers into a checksum: h starts at 0. For each question, in order, apply h = (h * 1000003 + a) mod 1000000007 for a = a1, a2, a3, a4, in this order. Return h as a number (0 when there is no question). Limits: 1 <= n <= 100000; 1 <= q <= 90000; 1 <= reach <= n; 0 <= removeTenths <= 6; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. There can be 90000 operations on 100000 stations, so rebuilding the components for every question is far too slow.

edges.self-loop: a self-loop is an odd cycle
edges.even-cycle: a cycle of even length is not an odd cycle
edges.odd-cycle: a triangle is an odd cycle
edges.removal-order: move the last link of the list into its place
edges.duplicate: a link that already exists is not added again

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Offline dynamic connectivity: a segment tree over the question times, with every link stored on the O(log q) nodes of its lifetime, and a union-find with parity and an undo stack that is walked depth first. The parity bit finds odd cycles, and the count of stations in odd components has to survive every undo. The exact removal rule (the last link moves into the freed place) fixes the lifetimes. The best simple answer rebuilds the union-find for every question, O(q * (n + links)): 20 s or more of CPU on the huge inputs. About 4 h for an expert who has done it before.

input.name: depotCostChecksum
input.signature: depotCostChecksum(n, window, maxCost, maxSetup, maxRate, seed) -> number
input.task: A rooted tree with n vertices numbered 0..n-1 (vertex 0 is the root) has a depot on every vertex. The tree, its edge costs and the depots are all built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. Step 1: for i = 1..n-1, draw r and set parent(i) = i - 1 - (r mod min(i, window)). So parent(i) < i. With window = 1 the tree is a single path 0-1-2-...-(n-1); a larger window gives a bushier tree. Step 2: for i = 1..n-1, draw r1 and then r2, and set down(i) = 1 + (r1 mod maxCost) and up(i) = r2 mod (maxCost + 1). down(i) is the cost of walking along the edge from parent(i) to i. up(i) is the cost of walking along the same edge from i to parent(i). The two directions of an edge can cost differently, and an upward cost of 0 is allowed. Step 3: for v = 0..n-1, draw r1 and then r2, and set setup(v) = r1 mod (maxSetup + 1) and rate(v) = r2 mod (maxRate + 1). A rate of 0 is allowed. The walk cost walk(u, v) is the sum of the edge costs along the unique path from u to v, where every edge is paid in the direction of the walk: up(i) when the walk goes from i to parent(i), down(i) when it goes from parent(i) to i. walk(u, u) = 0. The depot on u can serve vertex v at the price setup(u) + rate(u) * walk(u, v). A vertex may be served by its own depot. The service cost f(v) is the smallest price over all depots u. Fold f(0), f(1), ..., f(n-1) into a checksum: h starts at 0, and for each v in this order h = (h * 1000003 + f(v)) mod 1000000007. Return h as a number. Every f(v) and every intermediate product is an exact integer below 2^53. Limits: 1 <= n <= 50000; 1 <= window <= n; 1 <= maxCost <= 1000; 0 <= maxSetup <= 10^9; 0 <= maxRate <= 1000; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. The tree can be 50000 levels deep, so a recursive search can overflow the stack. Trying every depot for every vertex is far too slow.

edges.direction: the two directions of an edge can cost differently
edges.zero-up: an upward cost of 0 is allowed
edges.own-depot: a vertex may be served by its own depot

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Two techniques together: centroid decomposition (iterative, because the tree can be 50000 levels deep) and a convex hull of lines per centroid, with walk costs that differ by direction, so each vertex needs both a "to the centroid" and a "from the centroid" distance. The best simple answer walks the tree from every depot, O(n^2), 25 s or more of CPU on the largest inputs. About 4 h for an expert who has both ideas ready.

input.name: liftwell
input.task:
Implement liftwell(spec), a tick-by-tick simulation of a bank of lifts (elevators) in a building. spec is an object { floors, cars, people, events, dwell, flow, park, until }. floors is the number of floors; they are numbered 1 to floors (floor 1 is the lobby). cars is an array of cars { id, floor, cap, serves }: id is a string, floor is the start floor, cap is the weight the car can carry, serves is "all" (the default), "even" or "odd". people is an array of persons { id, t, from, to, w, vip }: id is a string, t is the tick at which the person arrives and presses the call button on floor from, to is the wanted floor, w is the weight (default 1), vip is true or false (default false). events is an optional array of { t, kind, car } (kinds below; car is a car id and only used by "out" and "back"). dwell (default 2), flow (default 2) and park (default 4) are whole numbers. until is the last tick that is simulated: the simulation runs the ticks 0, 1, 2, ..., until, in this order. Nothing in the input is checked beyond what this text says.

The function returns { people, cars, log }, three arrays of strings (their form is at the end).

WHAT A CAR KNOWS. A car has a floor, a direction (up, down or none), a door counter (the doors are open while it is above 0), a list of riders in the order in which they boarded, a count of the ticks it has been idle, its home floor (its start floor), and a count of moves (floors travelled) and of stops (times the doors were opened). A car serves a floor when serves is "all", or the floor is 1, or serves is "even" and the floor is even, or serves is "odd" and the floor is odd. A car is out of service while it is "out" (see EVENTS). The load of a car is the sum of the weights of its riders. A person is waiting from its arrival until it boards, and may be assigned to one car.

A TICK. In each tick, these steps run in this order: (1) the events of the tick; (2) the arrivals; (3) the dispatch; (4) every car, in the order of the array cars. Each car completes its whole step before the next car starts, so the later cars see the riders and the assignments that the earlier cars have changed in the same tick.

ARRIVALS. The persons whose t is the tick, in the order of the array people, become waiting. But a person is void (it never waits and is never considered again) when from or to is not a whole number between 1 and floors, or from equals to, or no car at all (in or out of service) serves both from and to.

TARGETS AND DIRECTION. The targets of a car are the to floors of its riders and the from floors of the waiting persons assigned to it. For the floor f of a car, "ups" is true when some target is above f and "downs" is true when some target is below f (a target at f itself counts for neither). The direction function of the car is: up when the car direction is up and ups is true; down when the car direction is down and downs is true; otherwise up when ups is true (also when both are true); otherwise down when downs is true; otherwise none. The word direction-rule below means this function. A person goes up when to is above from and down otherwise.

DISPATCH. Not done while a fire is on (see EVENTS). Take the waiting persons who are not assigned, oldest first (by t, then by position in people). For each one, in that order, look at every car that is not out of service and that serves both from and to. The cost of a car is: the distance |floor of the car - from|, plus 4 for every stop of the car, plus 6 when the car direction is up and from is below its floor, or the car direction is down and from is above its floor, plus 10 when 5 * load >= 4 * cap. A stop of the car is a different floor among the to floors of its riders and the from floors of the persons already assigned to it (also those assigned a moment ago in this same dispatch; floors that occur more than once count once). The person is assigned to the car with the lowest cost; on a tie the car with the smaller load; on a tie the car that comes first in the array. This is the dispatch-cost rule. A person with no such car stays unassigned and is looked at again in the next tick.

THE STEP OF A CAR. A car that is out of service does nothing. While a fire is on, the car follows FIRE (below). Otherwise:
1. Doors open (the counter is above 0): do the DOOR TICK (below).
2. Doors closed. Let sd be the direction-rule value of the car. The car stops when a rider has to equal its floor, or when there is a waiting person who is assigned to the car, has from equal to its floor, goes in the direction sd (or sd is none), and whose weight fits (load + w <= cap). When the car stops: add 1 to its stops, set idle to 0, write the log line "tick id open floor", set the door counter to dwell and do the DOOR TICK in the same tick.
3. Otherwise, when sd is not none: the car direction becomes sd, the car moves one floor in that direction (add 1 to moves), idle becomes 0.
4. Otherwise: the car direction becomes none; idle grows by 1; and when idle is now more than park and the floor of the car is not its home, the car moves one floor towards its home (add 1 to moves). A move towards home does not change idle.

THE DOOR TICK of a car at floor f. Let sd be the direction-rule value of the car. (a) Leaving: the riders whose to is f, in the order of the riders list and at most flow of them, leave the car: each becomes done with the done tick set to the tick, and a log line "tick id out person" is written; this happens before anyone boards. (b) Boarding: the candidates are the waiting persons who are assigned to this car and have from equal to f and go in the direction sd (when sd is none every one of them is a candidate). Order the candidates with vip persons first, then by arrival tick, then by position in people (this is the vip-priority rule). Go through them in that order: stop when flow persons have boarded in this tick; a candidate with load + w <= cap boards (it is added at the end of the riders list, its board tick and its car are set, it is no longer waiting for an assignment, and "tick id in person" is written); a candidate with load + w > cap does not board and loses its assignment (it is unassigned and the going through goes on with the next candidate; this is the weight-fit rule). (c) The car direction becomes the direction-rule value (computed again now). (d) If at least one person left or boarded in this tick, the door counter becomes dwell; otherwise it falls by 1.

EVENTS. The events of a tick are applied in the order of the array events, and only those with t equal to the tick. "out" with a car that is in service: the car goes out of service; all its riders become dropped with the done tick set to the tick (log line "tick id drop person", in the order of the riders), its riders list is emptied, its door counter becomes 0 and its direction none, and all persons assigned to it lose their assignment. "back" with a car that is out of service: the car is in service again, with idle 0 (everything else stays as it was). "fire": a fire starts (a fire that is already on stays on): the door counter of every car becomes 0 and every waiting person loses its assignment. "clear" while a fire is on: the fire ends; the direction of every car becomes none, and idle and the door counter become 0. All other events (also "out" for a car that is already out, "back" for one that is not out, "clear" without a fire, a car id that does not exist) do nothing.

FIRE. While a fire is on, each car that is in service does this in its step and nothing else: (1) when the door counter is above 0, or when the car is at floor 1 and has riders: if the door counter is 0, add 1 to the stops, write the log line "tick id open 1" and set the door counter to dwell; then at most flow riders (in the order of the riders list) leave: each becomes evac with the done tick set to the tick and the log line "tick id evac person" is written (they leave wherever their to is); the door counter becomes dwell when at least one rider left, else it falls by 1. (2) Otherwise, when the car is at floor 1: its direction becomes none. (3) Otherwise: the direction becomes down and the car moves one floor down (add 1 to moves). Persons that arrive during a fire wait, and the dispatch does not run. A car that is out of service does nothing and "back" during a fire only changes its out state.

THE RESULT. people has one string per person in the order of the array people, "id:state:car:board:done". state is future (arrival tick after until), void, waiting (arrived, not boarded), riding (in a car at the end), done, dropped or evac. car is the id of the car that carried the person, or "-" when the person never boarded. board and done are the ticks, or "-" when not set. cars has one string per car, in the order of cars, "id:floor:state:load:moves:stops", where state is "out" when the car is out of service, else "open" when its door counter is above 0, else its direction (up, down) or "idle" for none. log is the array of the log lines in the order in which they were written.

edges.direction-rule: The word direction-rule below means this function.
edges.fire-recall: While a fire is on, each car that is in service does this in its step and nothing else
edges.mixed-run: Each car completes its whole step before the next car starts

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A discrete-time simulation of lifts with a fixed order of work in every tick: events, arrivals, dispatch by a four-term cost with ties, a scan direction rule with targets from riders and assignments, door timing with extension, boarding with vip priority, weight fit and per-tick flow limits, zones by floor parity, parking, out-of-service and a fire recall. The reference is about 300 lines. An expert needs most of a working day to read the rules closely, write it and check it against worked traces.

input.name: palindromePieces
input.signature: palindromePieces(n, alpha, period, breaks, seed) -> [number, number]
input.task: A string s of length n over the letters 0..alpha-1 is built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. Step 1: for j = 0..period-1, draw r and set w[j] = r mod alpha. Step 2: for i = 0..n-1 set s[i] = w[i mod period]. Step 3: repeat `breaks` times, in order: draw r1, then draw r2, set p = r1 mod n, and replace s[p] by (s[p] + 1 + (r2 mod (alpha - 1))) mod alpha. A break always changes the letter, and a later break can change a position that an earlier break has already changed. A palindrome is a non-empty string that reads the same forwards and backwards; a single letter is a palindrome. Cut s into consecutive non-empty pieces so that every piece is a palindrome. Every letter belongs to exactly one piece, and the whole string can be a single piece (a cut into one piece). Let m be the smallest possible number of pieces. Two cuts are different when their sets of cut positions are different. Count the different cuts into exactly m pieces: there can be several different ways, and the count can be huge. Return the array [m, c], where c is that count modulo 1000000007. Limits: 1 <= n <= 600000; 2 <= alpha <= 4; 1 <= period <= 8; 0 <= breaks <= 1000; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646. A string such as "aaaa..." has a palindromic suffix of every length at every position, so any method that looks at all palindromic suffixes of every prefix is far too slow, and so is a quadratic dynamic programme over all pieces.

edges.whole: the whole string can be a single piece
edges.ties: there can be several different ways
edges.break: a break always changes the letter

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: A palindromic tree together with series links (the suffix palindromes of a prefix fall into O(log n) arithmetic series), run over a (minimum, count) pair instead of a single number, so ties between series have to be merged exactly. Strings such as "aaaa..." have a palindrome of every length at every position, so the plain walk over all palindromic suffixes is O(n^2): 50 s or more of CPU on the huge inputs. About 4.5 h for an expert who knows the series-link technique.

input.name: countMudPaths
input.signature: countMudPaths(a, b, c, d, k, seed) -> number
input.task: A token walks on the integer grid from (0,0) to (a,b). Every step moves it one cell right (x + 1) or one cell up (y + 1). Some cells are mud. The mud cells are built from a pseudo-random generator, so the input stays small. The generator draws x_0 = seed and x_(i+1) = (x_i * 48271 + 11) mod 2147483647 for i = 0, 1, 2, ... (exact integer arithmetic; every product is below 2^47). Each draw returns the new x. For j = 0..k-1, in order, draw r1 and then r2, and set px = r1 mod (a + 1) and py = px + (r2 mod (c + d + 3)) - (d + 1). A drawn cell with y < 0 or y > b is discarded. Otherwise (px, py) is a mud cell. The same cell can be drawn twice; it is one mud cell. A path from (0,0) to (a,b) is valid when every cell it visits, the start and the end included, satisfies both rules: (1) the cell is not a mud cell: a mud cell may not be visited; (2) -d <= y - x <= c, so the path can never go above the line y = x + c and can never go below the line y = x - d. Return the number of valid paths modulo 998244353, as a number. There may be no path at all (for instance when the start, the end or a whole barrier of cells is mud, or when (a,b) itself lies outside the band), and then the answer is 0. Limits: 1 <= a, b <= 200000; 0 <= c, d <= 400000; 0 <= k <= 300; 1 <= seed <= 2147483646; a + b <= 30 * (c + d + 2). The grid has up to 4 * 10^10 cells, so a dynamic programme over the grid is far too slow. Products modulo 998244353 can reach 10^18, which a double cannot hold exactly.

edges.ceiling: above the line y = x + c
edges.two-sided: below the line y = x - d
edges.mud-block: a mud cell may not be visited
edges.blocked: there may be no path at all
edges.outside: a drawn cell with y < 0 or y > b is discarded

tier.name: supreme
tier.basis: Two combinatorial arguments together, modulo a prime. Paths between two parallel lines are counted by the reflection principle with an alternating sum over all repeated reflections (a single reflection is wrong), and the mud cells are removed by inclusion and exclusion over the cells sorted by position, each pair needing its own two-line count. Products modulo 998244353 reach 10^18, so the multiplication has to be exact. The grid dynamic programme costs about 10^10 cells: 45 s or more of CPU on the huge inputs. About 3.5 h for an expert who knows both arguments.

input.name: typeset
input.task:
Implement typeset(text, options), a small typesetter for monospaced text. It returns an array of strings, the lines of the page. options is an object { width, align, indent, hang, hyphenate, columns, gutter, exceptions }. width is a whole number from 8 to 80. align is "left" (the default), "right", "center" or "justify". indent (default 0) and hang (default 0) are whole numbers from 0 to 8. hyphenate (default false) is a boolean. columns (default 1) is 1, 2 or 3. gutter (default 2) is a whole number from 1 to 6. exceptions (default none) is an array of strings made of lowercase letters a-z and hyphens.

WIDTH OF TEXT. Every width below is measured in cells. Each code point of a string takes the cells given by its number: U+0300 to U+036F (combining marks) take 0 cells; U+1100 to U+115F, U+2E80 to U+A4CF, U+AC00 to U+D7A3, U+FF01 to U+FF60 and U+FFE0 to U+FFE6 take 2 cells; every other code point takes 1 cell. The width of a string is the sum over its code points (iterate by code point, not by UTF-16 unit). A space is 1 cell.

PARAGRAPHS AND WORDS. First every "\r\n" and every single "\r" in text becomes "\n". A line is blank when it holds only spaces and tabs (or nothing). Paragraphs are the maximal runs of non-blank lines, so one or more blank lines separate two paragraphs, and blank lines at the start and the end are ignored. The words of a paragraph are the pieces of its lines joined by one space and cut at every run of spaces and tabs. A text without any word gives the empty array. Nothing else is whitespace: in particular U+00A0 is an ordinary character of a word.
The lines of the result are the lines of the first paragraph, then one empty string "", then the lines of the second paragraph, and so on: exactly one empty string between two paragraphs, whatever the number of blank lines in the text.

KINDS OF PARAGRAPH. Look at the first word of a paragraph that has two or more words. If it is "#" the paragraph is a level 1 heading; if it is "##" it is a level 2 heading; if it is ">" it is a quote. That first word is then removed and is not part of the text. Every other paragraph is plain (a paragraph of the single word "#" is plain and shows "#"). The rest of the words go through GLUE below.
GLUE. Process the words in order with a pending prefix that starts as the empty string. A word made only of characters from . , ; : ! ? ) (one or more of them), when at least one word has already been output and the last output word is not "//", is appended to the last output word. A word made only of ( characters, when it is not the last word and the next word is not "//", is added to the pending prefix. Any other word is output as the pending prefix followed by the word, and the pending prefix becomes empty. (So "( fig ) ," becomes the one word "(fig),".) A word of ( characters that is the last word, or is followed by "//", is output like any other word.

THE PIECES OF A WORD. A word is split into pieces, and after each piece but the last there is a break point of one kind: hard, soft or auto. The text of the word is the pieces written one after another.
- A word that holds an underscore "_" that is not directly preceded by a backslash is a no-break word: every such underscore shows as a space, every "~" is removed, and every "\_" shows as a plain "_". A no-break word is one single piece and has no break point (it may hold spaces, which count in its width).
- Otherwise a "\_" shows as a plain "_" and the following applies. A "~" is a soft break point when there is a character directly before it and a character directly after it in the word, neither of which is "~", and the piece before it is not empty (that is, it does not come directly after a hard break point). The "~" itself is never shown. Every other "~" is removed without effect. A word that is empty after the removal of its "~" is dropped from the paragraph.
- A "-" is a hard break point, placed after the hyphen, when the character before it and the character after it are both ASCII letters or digits (for this rule the word is taken with each "\_" already replaced by "_" and with its "~" still in place, so a "~" next to a "-" stops the break). The hyphen stays at the end of its piece. Any other "-" is an ordinary character.
- Automatic hyphenation happens only when options.hyphenate is true, and only for a word that has exactly one piece and holds no "-" and no "~". Let core be the word without its leading characters from ( " ' and without its trailing characters from . , ; : ! ? ) " '. If core has at least 4 characters and all of them are ASCII letters, its automatic break points are found as follows. Compare in lowercase. If core, in lowercase, equals an entry of options.exceptions with its hyphens removed, the break points are the places of the hyphens in that entry (a hyphen after n letters is a break point between letter n - 1 and letter n of core, counting letters from 0; positions 0 and the length of core are ignored; when several entries match, the last of them is used); this is used for any length of core of 4 or more. Otherwise, if core has fewer than 7 letters there are none. Otherwise let L be the length of core and consider every position p from 3 to L - 3 (a break between letter p - 1 and letter p, counting letters from 0, so at least 3 letters stay on each side). The letters a e i o u are vowels, and y is a vowel unless it is the letter 0 of core; every other letter is a consonant. The digraphs are ch sh th ph and ck. Position p is a break point in exactly these three cases: (1) letter p - 1 is a vowel, letter p is a consonant and letter p + 1 is a vowel; (2) letter p - 1 is a vowel, letters p and p + 1 form a digraph and letter p + 2 is a vowel; (3) letters p - 1 and p are consonants, letter p - 2 and letter p + 1 are vowels, and letters p - 1 and p do not form a digraph. The pieces then are the parts of the word between these break points, all of kind auto (leading and trailing punctuation stay with the first and last piece).

LINES OF A PARAGRAPH. The available width of a line is the width of the layout (see the end) minus the prefix of the line. The prefix is 0 for every line when align is "right" or "center". When align is "left" or "justify" the prefix of the first line is indent, and the prefix of every other line is the continuation prefix, which is hang, except for a paragraph that starts with a list marker: when a plain or quote paragraph has two or more words and its first word (after GLUE) is made of digits followed by "." or ")", or is "-" or "+", the continuation prefix is indent + the width of that first word + 1, and hang is not used. The prefix is not part of the line width used below; it is only subtracted from the available width.
Lines are filled greedily, word by word, from left to right. The current line is a list of items; its used width is the sum of the widths of its items plus 1 for each gap between two items. For each word, in order, repeat the following steps until the whole word is placed:
1. If the word is "//": the current line ends as a forced line and nothing else happens; if the current line has no item, an empty line is produced (it is shown as ""). A forced line is not justified and is not a mark-break line, and the next line starts empty.
2. Let rest be all the remaining pieces of the word written together. If used width + 1 (when the line has an item) + width of rest is at most the available width, rest becomes one item of the line and the word is done.
3. Otherwise look for a break point inside the rest. For k from the number of remaining pieces minus 1 down to 1, consider ending the line after the first k pieces: the candidate text is those k pieces, plus one "-" when the break point after piece k is soft or auto (a hard break point has its hyphen in the piece already). The candidate fits when used width + 1 (when the line has an item) + width of the candidate text is at most the available width. The first candidate that fits (so the largest k) is chosen. But a soft or auto break point is not allowed when the two lines directly before this line in the paragraph both ended with a soft or auto break (a mark break); only hard break points are considered then. If a candidate is chosen, the candidate text becomes the last item of the current line, the line ends, and the word continues with the pieces after the first k.
4. If no candidate fits and the current line has an item, the line ends (not forced, not a mark break) and the word starts again from step 2 on the next line.
5. If no candidate fits and the current line has no item, the first piece is cut: take characters from its start while the total width stays at most the available width, but always at least one character. That part becomes the only item of the line, the line ends without a "-", and the rest of the first piece (if any) stays as the first piece of the word, with its break point; if nothing is left of the first piece, the word continues with the next piece.
At the end of the paragraph a current line that has an item ends as the last line. A line that ends after a chosen candidate with a soft or auto break point is a mark-break line; a hard break point, a forced cut and a plain end of line are not.

WIDOWS. After the lines of a plain or quote paragraph are made, if the paragraph has at least 3 lines, the last line has exactly one item whose width is at most 3, neither the last line nor the line before it is forced, the line before it has at least 2 items, its last item is not a part of a word that goes on in the next line (an item made by a chosen candidate or by a cut is such a part), and the width of that last item + 1 + the width of the item of the last line is at most the width of the layout minus the continuation prefix (0 when align is "right" or "center"), then that last item moves from the line before to the front of the last line. The prefix of the last line is the continuation prefix.

ALIGNMENT. The text of a line is its items joined by single spaces. align "left": the prefix, then the text. "right": spaces so that the line ends at the width of the layout, then the text. "center": floor((width of the layout - width of the text) / 2) spaces, then the text. "justify": the prefix, then the text with its gaps made wider, but only for a line that is not the last line of its paragraph, is not forced and has at least 2 items; any other line of a justified paragraph is written like "left". An empty line is the empty string.
JUSTIFY. Let extra be the available width minus the width of the text. The gaps are the spaces between two neighbouring items. The weight of a gap is 2 when the item before it, after removing any closing characters from " ' ) ] at its end, ends with one of . ! ? : and otherwise 1. Let T be the sum of the weights. Each gap first gets floor(extra * weight / T) extra spaces. The left-over spaces (extra minus the sum of the shares), fewer than the number of gaps, go one each to the gaps with the largest value of (extra * weight) mod T; among equal values the gap that is closer to the end of the line comes first. A gap then holds 1 + its extra spaces.

HEADINGS. A heading is laid out with the width of the layout, never with indent, hang, list markers, hyphenation or the widow treatment. A level 1 heading is written in capitals (every word through toUpperCase) and is centered; a level 2 heading is written as it is and aligned left with prefix 0. After its lines comes one more line: the widest line of the heading (its width after removing spaces at both ends) as that many "=" characters for level 1, centered like the lines ("center" rule), and as that many "-" characters from the start of the line for level 2.
QUOTES. A quote is laid out like a plain paragraph with the layout width reduced by 2 (and with the same align, indent, hang and list rule), and every line of it is then written as "> " followed by the line, with any spaces at the end of the result removed (so an empty line becomes ">").

COLUMNS. The width of a column is the width option when columns is 1. Otherwise it is floor((width - gutter * (columns - 1)) / columns), and this is the width of the layout in every rule above. All paragraphs are laid out into one list of lines, as above. When columns is 1 that list is the result. Otherwise let n be its length: column i (counting from 0) gets the next n div columns lines of the list, plus 1 more if i < n mod columns. In every column, empty lines at its top are removed. The result has as many rows as the tallest column; a row is the cells of the columns, each cell padded with spaces at its end to the width of the layout (an absent cell is all spaces), joined by gutter spaces, with the spaces at the end of the whole row removed.
